title: How a Country Uses Its Land
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Land is a limited resource, and how a country uses it shapes its economy, its landscape and its wildlife. The imaginary country of Altonia has four main regions, and a recent land survey measured the share of each region covered by forest, farmland and settlements. The results, drawn as pie charts, show strikingly different patterns, which reflect the geography of each region and the way its people have chosen to live. This passage describes the four regions and explains the problems that each one faces, before looking at the national policy that the government has proposed in order to protect its most valuable land.

In the Northern Valley, seven tenths of the land is covered by forest, and the rest is divided between farms and a few small towns, with farms covering about twice as much as the towns. The valley is steep and cold, and the soil is thin, so farming has never been easy. The forests supply timber, and the clean water that flows from them is used by the cities in the south. The main problem is the pressure to cut more trees, since timber is profitable, and conservation groups have asked the government to protect the oldest woods from cutting.

The Eastern Plain is the opposite. Four fifths of the land is farmland, producing most of the country's wheat and sugar beet, and forest and settlements each cover only a tenth. The soil is deep and rich, and the land is flat, which makes machines easy to use. But farming on such a large scale has costs: the hedges and ponds where wild animals once lived have been removed, and chemicals used on the fields have polluted several streams. Farmers say that they must grow as much as possible to compete with imports, though some have started to plant strips of wild flowers along the edges of their fields.

The coastal region is more balanced: its land is divided into three almost equal parts, one third forest, one third farmland and one third towns and settlements. Many people live here, because the climate is mild and the ports bring trade, and the towns have grown rapidly. Each year they spread a little further over the farms, and the farmers complain that their best fields are being lost to houses and car parks. Planners have to decide how much further the towns may expand, knowing that every new house brings jobs and homes but also takes away land that cannot easily be replaced.

The Highland Plateau has a simple pattern: half of its land is forest and the other half is grassland, used for grazing sheep and goats, and there are hardly any buildings at all. Only a few thousand people live there, in scattered villages, and the roads are poor. Herders move their animals between summer and winter pastures, as their families have done for centuries. The plateau is the quietest region of the country, and its wildlife, which includes wolves and eagles, is the richest. The problem here is the opposite of the one on the coast: young people are leaving for the towns, and some villages have been abandoned.

Dr Rafael Mendes, a geographer, argues that every region needs a plan to protect the land that matters most. He proposes that forests of high value should be protected by law, that the best farmland should be kept for farming, and that towns should be encouraged to grow upwards instead of outwards, building taller apartments rather than spreading houses over fields. Taller buildings house more people on less land, he says, and they make public transport easier to run, because passengers live closer to the stations. Critics reply that many people prefer houses with gardens and will not accept the change.

The government has accepted part of his proposal. A new law will forbid building on the best farmland, and a fund will pay farmers who protect hedges and ponds. It has not yet agreed to protect all the old forests, because the timber industry has argued that this would cost thousands of jobs. Discussion continues, and a final decision is expected within two years. In the meantime, the survey will be repeated every five years, so that anyone can see whether the pie charts are changing and whether the promises made are being kept.
